**ID:** MN 138 (PTS MN iii 223)

**Title (Pali):** Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** A Summary Recital and its Analysis

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Uddesavibhaṅga Sutta* (MN 138, PTS MN iii 223) is set at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The discourse opens with the Buddha announcing that he will teach both a brief summary (*uddesa*) and an exposition (*vibhaṅga*): a bhikkhu should examine phenomena in such a manner that his consciousness is neither scattered and distracted externally nor stuck internally, and by not clinging does not become agitated [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Having recited only this concise summary, the Buddha unexpectedly rises and retreats, leaving the monks unable to penetrate its meaning [SuttaCentral; Caudron 2000]. The monks approach Venerable Mahākaccāna, who rebukes them for failing to question the Buddha face-to-face, but nevertheless provides an elaborate, analytical explanation [Caudron 2000; Nyanaponika et al. 2003].

In his analysis, Mahākaccāna explains that consciousness is "distracted externally" when it pursues sensory objects across all six senses, while it is "stuck internally" (*ajjhattaṃ saṇṭhita*) when it clings to the subtle gratification of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*s) [Anālayo 2003; Wen 2011]. Furthermore, non-agitation through non-clinging is analyzed through the five aggregates: agitation arises when a practitioner identifies an aggregate as self and laments its inevitable alteration, whereas an instructed noble disciple abandons this identification and avoids anguish [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Sujato 2012]. The cessation of such agitation eliminates future birth, aging, death, and suffering [Radich 2007]. Scholars observe that the *uddesa–vibhaṅga* format closely resembles the methodology later systematized in early Abhidhamma texts and the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, prompting scholars such as G. C. Pande to argue for a relatively late date based on formal and doctrinal characteristics [Anālayo 2014; Radich 2007].

Curated parallels include a discourse in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 164), Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT sutta 52), and thematic counterparts in the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22.7) and the Chinese *Saṁyukta-āgama* (SĀ 43, SĀ 66) [SuttaCentral]. Computational matching via DharmaNexus corroborates these alignments, identifying substantial correspondences with Chinese Āgama texts (T 26) as well as internal Pali reuse with the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), and structurally related expositions by Mahākaccāna in the *Madhupiṇḍika Sutta* (MN 18) and *Mahākaccānabhaddekaratta Sutta* (MN 133) [DharmaNexus].
